plan.chapterName: Anton, Bivens, and Davis. Calculus, 10th Edition, Figure 14.3.3
plan.contextChunk: This figure shows a polar rectangle R, the fundamental building block for polar double integration. The region R is bounded by two circular arcs r = 1.5 and r = 2 (solid blue curves) and two rays theta = pi/6 and theta = pi/4 (dashed red lines), forming a curved quadrilateral shaded in light blue and labeled R. The figure introduces the polar rectangle as the analogue of the Cartesian rectangle for setting up double integrals in polar coordinates, showing how its curved sides arise from the constant-r and constant-theta boundary conditions.

interactionPlan.concept: A polar rectangle is bounded by lines of constant radius (circular arcs) and constant angle (straight rays), serving as the fundamental area element for polar double integrals.
elements: horizontal black line representing the polar axis
origin point (pole) at the left end of the axis
red dashed ray for lower angle bound, initially labeled θ = π/6
red dashed ray for upper angle bound, initially labeled θ = π/4
solid blue circular arc for inner radial bound, initially labeled r = 1.5
solid blue circular arc for outer radial bound, initially labeled r = 2
light blue shaded region R enclosed by the arcs and rays, labeled 'R' in the center
straight-sided Cartesian rectangle outline (visible only when toggled)

interactions.label: Inner radius (r1)
interactions.teaches: The inner boundary is a path of constant radius, forming a circular arc rather than a straight line.

interactions.label: Outer radius (r2)
interactions.teaches: Increasing the outer radius expands the region outward along the rays, extending its radial depth.

interactions.label: Start angle (θ1)
interactions.teaches: The lower boundary is defined by a constant angle, forming a straight ray originating from the pole.

interactions.label: End angle (θ2)
interactions.teaches: Increasing the upper angle widens the region's angular sweep without changing its distance from the origin.

interactions.label: Cartesian overlay
interactions.teaches: Unlike a Cartesian rectangle with four straight sides, a polar rectangle has two curved sides because its 'top' and 'bottom' bounds follow circular paths.

demo_steps.title: The Polar Rectangle
demo_steps.narration: Region R is defined by constant bounds in r and θ. It forms a curved quadrilateral that acts as the basic grid cell for polar integration.

demo_steps.title: Adjusting radial bounds
demo_steps.narration: Increasing the outer radius stretches R outward. Its top and bottom boundaries are circular arcs because they are defined by a constant distance from the pole.

demo_steps.title: Adjusting angular bounds
demo_steps.narration: Increasing the end angle sweeps R wider. Its left and right boundaries are straight rays because they represent paths of constant angle.

demo_steps.title: Cartesian vs Polar
demo_steps.narration: Overlaying a standard Cartesian rectangle highlights the geometric difference: holding r constant traces a curve, which is why polar area elements depend on their distance from the origin.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: A polar rectangle has straight sides along its angular bounds (rays) but curved sides along its radial bounds (arcs), fundamentally distinguishing it from a Cartesian rectangle.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Place the origin at the bottom left with the polar axis extending horizontally to the right. The two red dashed rays emanate from the origin. The two blue solid arcs are concentric with the origin. Region R is shaded a distinct light blue. When cartesianOverlay is true, draw a dashed, straight-sided rectangular box aligned at the inner-start corner (r1, θ1) with dimensions Δr by r1*Δθ to visually contrast straight Cartesian edges against the polar region's curved arcs. Math labels should dynamically update if the generator supports formatting the slider values as fractions of pi or decimals.

plan.authoredInteractions:
- Sliders for r1 and r2 (pre-filled 1.5 and 2): stretch or shrink the two bounding arcs and watch the curved quadrilateral R resize between them while the angular bounds stay fixed
- Sliders for θ1 and θ2 (pre-filled π/6 and π/4): rotate the two bounding rays and watch R sweep through the new angular extent while the radial bounds stay fixed
- Toggle to overlay a straight-sided Cartesian rectangle of the same Δr × Δθ dimensions at the same corner — shows why R is only an "analogue" of a rectangle: two of its sides are curved because r is held constant on a circular arc rather than a straight line

discrepancies: The label for the outer radius reads 'r = 2.0' instead of 'r = 2' due to forced decimal formatting
The angle labels (θ = π/4, θ = π/6) are placed very far out along the rays (radius > 3), whereas the source figure places them closer to the middle/origin
The bounding arcs (solid blue lines) in the source extend much further beyond the dashed boundary rays than they do in the generated figure
evaluation.notes: The generated figure is an excellent interactive teaching tool with comprehensive controls, but has minor label formatting and placement discrepancies compared to the static source.
action_items: Format the radius labels to drop the '.0' for whole numbers (e.g., use `Number(r2.toFixed(1)).toString()` instead of `r2.toFixed(1)`).
Decrease the hardcoded `rRayLbl` radius for the angle labels so they are positioned closer to the origin, matching the source.
Increase the angular extension of the blue arcs past the boundary rays (currently `+ 0.22` and `- 0.2`); the source draws them extending significantly further to emphasize they are continuous curves.
